decision.location: Experiments, Experiment 1: Welfare spending, p. 6 (lines 455-466); Treatment effect heterogeneity, p. 9 (lines 571-587); References, pp. 13-14
decision.quote:
Experiment 1: Welfare spending
Our first experiment replicates a classic question wording
experiment. Control subjects are asked whether we are
spending too little, about right, or too much on “welfare.”
Treatment subjects are asked the same question about
“Assistance to the poor” or “Caring for the poor.” The
General Social Survey (GSS) has conducted this experiment
every other year since 1984; we use the 2014 GSS estimate
as the baseline result. This experiment behaves on Lucid
much as it does on MTurk and the GSS – a large increase in
support for redistribution when the question is phrased as
assistance or caring for the poor rather than as “welfare.”
decision.reason: In Experiment 1 (Welfare spending), the authors empirically conduct the classic welfare versus assistance/caring for the poor question-wording experiment on Lucid (N = 3,504) and compare the treatment effect estimates against the 2014 General Social Survey (GSS) baseline result (and 2016 GSS conditional average treatment effects by race/ethnicity). However, the primary source text and reference list do not cite or identify any specific published original paper or bibliographic dataset entry for the recurring GSS welfare spending experiment (nor for what p. 9 refers to as 'the original iteration of this experiment'), leaving authors, year, title, and DOI blank in the blind candidate. The sole welfare-related citation in the section, Gilens (1996), is explicitly described as subsequent work identifying race as a moderator ('Though this is not one of the factors theorized to condition the phrasing treatment effect in the original iteration of this experiment, race has since been identified as perhaps the single most important influencing factor in position on welfare spending (Gilens, 1996)'). Shipped row 462 (Berinsky, Huber, and Lenz 2012, 10.1093/pan/mpr057) is the methodological validation template removed in prior adjudication (prior state file absent). The precise unresolved question is what specific source-backed original bibliographic identity (authors, year, title) corresponds to the GSS welfare spending experiment in Experiment 1.

corrected_value.title: The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice.

decision.location: Experiments, Experiment 2: Asian Disease problem, pp. 6-7 (lines 468-500); Table 1, p. 4 (lines 287-288); References, p. 14 (lines 1005-1006)
decision.quote:
Experiment 2: Asian Disease problem
Our second experiment is also a classic, this time of the
behavioral economics literature. Tversky and Kahneman
(1981) show that people take the riskier option when in a
“loss frame” rather than a “gain frame.” Subjects are asked
to “Imagine that your country is preparing for the outbreak
of an unusual disease, which is expected to kill 600 people.
Two alternative programs to combat the disease have been
proposed.” Subjects in the control condition are told: “If
Program A is adopted, 200 people will be saved. If Program
B is adopted, there is one-third probability that 600 people
will be saved, and two-third probability that no people will
be saved.” Subjects in the treatment group (the “mortality
frame”) are told: “If Program A is adopted, 400 people will
die. If Program B is adopted there is one-third probability
that nobody will die, and two-third probability that 600 people will die.”
decision.reason: In Experiment 2, the authors empirically re-test Tversky and Kahneman's (1981) Asian Disease framing experiment on a new Lucid sample, scaling treatment effect estimates by the mean and standard deviation of the original experiment and comparing the gain-versus-loss framing effect across the original undergraduate sample, MTurk, and Lucid (Figure 2). The original work is explicitly identified in the text, Table 1, and the reference list as Tversky A and Kahneman D (1981) 'The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice', Science 211(4481): 453-458 (no DOI printed). The sole shipped row (input_row_index 462: Berinsky, Huber, and Lenz 2012, 10.1093/pan/mpr057, removed in prior adjudication; prior state file absent) is a 2012 Political Analysis methodological paper on MTurk that supplies the validation template, not an alternate report of Tversky and Kahneman (1981), and none of the sibling targets (0, 2, 3, 4) duplicate this 1981 original.

decision.location: Experiments, Experiment 5: Healthcare rumors, p. 9 (lines 539-561); Treatment effect heterogeneity, p. 9 (lines 606-619); Discussion, p. 12 (lines 736-750); References, p. 13 (lines 875-877)
decision.quote:
We conclude our set of five experiments with a note of caution. We attempted to replicate Berinsky’s 2017 experiment
on belief in rumors surrounding the Affordable Care Act
(ACA), specifically the false rumor that the ACA would
create “death panels” that would make end-of-life decisions
for patients without their consent. In the original experiment (conducted in 2010 on a sample provided by Survey
Sampling International (SSI)), a large portion of the sample
believed the rumor, and corrections delivered by
Republicans, Democrats, and Nonpartisan groups were all
effective in correcting false beliefs.
decision.reason: In Experiment 5, the authors empirically re-test Berinsky's (2017) experiment on correcting ACA 'death panel' misinformation using a new Lucid sample, comparing baseline rumor belief, average treatment effects (Figure 2), and partisan conditional average treatment effects (Figure 5) directly against the original 2010 SSI sample reported in Berinsky (2017). The reference list identifies this target as Berinsky AJ (2017) 'Rumors and health care reform: Experiments in political misinformation', British Journal of Political Science 47(2): 241-262 (no DOI printed). Although Adam J. Berinsky is also first author of shipped row 462 (Berinsky, Huber, and Lenz 2012, 10.1093/pan/mpr057, 'Evaluating Online Labor Markets for Experimental Research: Amazon.com's Mechanical Turk', Political Analysis 20(3): 351-368, removed in prior adjudication; prior state file absent), the two works are substantively distinct studies—indeed, p. 6 (line 447) explicitly notes that the Berinsky (2017) experiment 'has not been previously replicated on an MTurk sample'—so report equivalence does not apply.

corrected_value.authors: Bridgeman, B., Hendry, D., & Stark, L.
corrected_value.title: Failure to detect displacement of the visual world during saccadic eye movements

decision.quote: However, performance declines the closer in time displacements were presented to saccade onset. This result replicates previous findings ( Bridgeman, Hendry, & Stark, 1975 ; Zimmermann, 2020 ). One can also see that the peak of suppression at the time of saccade onset is lower in no context sessions than in context sessions. In other words, after performing context trials, subjects were better able to discriminate the direction of the background displacement. Figure 3 A shows results averaged across all subjects with discrimination performance measured in the baseline range (shown in purple) and within the perisaccadic range (shown in orange). The reduction in discrimination performance in the perisaccadic range can be seen clearly for both session types. A nonparametric repeated measures ANOVA with the factors “stimulus time” (baseline/perisaccadic) and “session type” (“no context”/“context”) revealed a significant main effect for the factor “stimulus time” (F(1,5) = 18.85, p = 0.007), confirming the well-known suppression of displacements during saccades ( Bridgeman, Hendry, & Stark, 1975 ).
decision.reason: In Experiment 1 (N = 6 new participants), the authors measure displacement discrimination performance as a function of time relative to saccade onset and run a 2 x 2 nonparametric repeated-measures ANOVA with factors 'stimulus time' (baseline vs. perisaccadic) and 'session type' (no context vs. context). In Results experiment 1, they explicitly report both that the perisaccadic decline in displacement detection 'replicates previous findings ( Bridgeman, Hendry, & Stark, 1975 ; Zimmermann, 2020 )' and that the significant main effect of 'stimulus time' (F(1,5) = 18.85, p = 0.007) confirms 'the well-known suppression of displacements during saccades ( Bridgeman, Hendry, & Stark, 1975 )', whereas the main effect of 'session type' and interaction confirm the context dependency of Zimmermann (2020). Under the codebook and pilot objections (Coleman), explicit empirical confirmation of a specific finding in Results is a valid retested target rather than mere background. The reference list provides the full identity: Bridgeman, B., Hendry, D., & Stark, L. (1975), 'Failure to detect displacement of the visual world during saccadic eye movements', Vision Research, 15(6), 719-722 (no DOI printed). The sole shipped row (input_row_index 2268: Zimmermann 2020, 10.7554/elife.49700, 'Saccade suppression depends on context') is a distinct 2020 study by a different author in eLife testing contextual modulation rather than an alternate report of Bridgeman et al. (1975). No prior adjudication or state files exist for this work.
